# Lab 8 — Supply Chain: Signing, Tampering, and Attestation

## Task 1 — Sign an image, then try to swap it

### Signed digest

I pushed `bkimminich/juice-shop:v20.0.0` to the local registry and signed the local-registry digest, not the Docker Hub digest.
The signed digest was:

```text
localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe
```

I selected it by filtering the image repo digests for the `localhost:5000/` registry and saved it in:

```text
labs/lab8/results/juice-shop-digest.txt
```

![Local registry digest selected for signing](data:image/png;base64,)

### Successful verification of the original digest

The signed digest was verified with:

```bash
cosign verify   --key labs/lab8/keys/cosign.pub   --insecure-ignore-tlog   --allow-insecure-registry   "$DIGEST"
```

The successful output included:

```text
The cosign claims were validated
The signatures were verified against the specified public key
```

The verified payload showed the signature was bound to this image digest:

```json
{
  "critical": {
    "identity": {
      "docker-reference": "localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe"
    },
    "image": {
      "docker-manifest-digest": "sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe"
    },
    "type": "https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1"
  }
}
```

The verification output was saved to:

```text
labs/lab8/results/verify-original.json
```

![Cosign verification succeeded for the original digest](data:image/png;base64,)

### Swapped image verification failure

I replaced the image behind the same tag with `alpine:3.20`.
The tag stayed the same:

```text
localhost:5000/juice-shop:v20.0.0
```

but it now resolved to a different digest:

```text
localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:c64c687cbea9300178b30c95835354e34c4e4febc4badfe27102879de0483b5e
```

Before and after:

```text
signed:
localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe

now:
localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:c64c687cbea9300178b30c95835354e34c4e4febc4badfe27102879de0483b5e
```

![Signed digest versus tampered digest](data:image/png;base64,)

Verification of the new digest failed with this exact error:

```text
Error: no signatures found
error during command execution: no signatures found
```

The output was saved to:

```text
labs/lab8/results/verify-tampered.txt
```

![Cosign verification failed for the swapped image](data:image/png;base64,)

### Original digest still verified

After the tag was overwritten, the original signed digest still verified successfully.
The output again included:

```text
The signatures were verified against the specified public key
```

![Original digest still verifies after tag swap](data:image/png;base64,)

### Explanation

A tag such as `v20.0.0` is a mutable pointer, but a digest identifies exact image content.
In this lab, the same tag first pointed to digest `sha256:28870b9d...` and later pointed to `sha256:c64c687c...`.
Cosign noticed the swap because the signature was bound to the original digest, not to the tag name.
If signatures were bound only to tags, an attacker who could replace the image behind a trusted tag could keep the trusted name while changing the actual content.

## Task 2 — Attach the SBOM as an attestation

A signature proves that the image digest was signed.
An attestation adds signed information about that digest.
For this task, I attached two attestations to the original signed digest:

```text
localhost:5000/juice-shop@sha256:28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe
```

### SBOM attestation component count

The CycloneDX SBOM from Lab 4 was used as the predicate:

```text
labs/lab4/juice-shop.cdx.json
```

The original SBOM component count was:

```text
3069
```

After verifying the attestation, I extracted the SBOM predicate to:

```text
labs/lab8/results/sbom-from-attestation.json
```

The extracted SBOM component count was also:

```text
3069
```

| Source | Component count |
|---|---:|
| Lab 4 CycloneDX SBOM | 3069 |
| SBOM extracted from verified attestation | 3069 |

The counts match, so the SBOM recovered from the attestation matches the Lab 4 SBOM at the component-count level requested by the lab.

![SBOM component counts from original and attestation](data:image/png;base64,)

### Predicate types

Both `predicateType` values were read from verified attestation payloads.

| Attestation | Cosign type used | Verified `predicateType` |
|---|---|---|
| CycloneDX SBOM | `cyclonedx` | `https://cyclonedx.org/bom` |
| SLSA provenance | `slsaprovenance` | `https://slsa.dev/provenance/v0.2` |

![Verified attestation predicate types](data:image/png;base64,)

### Decoded statement fields

The decoded CycloneDX statement contained these fields:

```json
{
  "_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v0.1",
  "subject": [
    {
      "name": "localhost:5000/juice-shop",
      "digest": {
        "sha256": "28870b9d2bec49e605d6ebbf4b22ed1ec1ca0a72347ef19217bbbb21ea44e3fe"
      }
    }
  ],
  "predicateType": "https://cyclonedx.org/bom"
}
```

`_type` identifies the outer document as an in-toto Statement, and Cosign filled it in.
`subject` identifies the image digest the attestation describes; I supplied that digest as the target to `cosign attest`, and Cosign placed it into the statement.
`predicateType` came from the `--type cyclonedx` option, which Cosign mapped to `https://cyclonedx.org/bom`.
The predicate content itself came from `--predicate labs/lab4/juice-shop.cdx.json`.

For the SLSA attestation, the predicate body contained the builder, build type, and config source.
Cosign wrapped that predicate body in the attestation statement, so I did not manually provide `_type` or `subject` in the provenance JSON.

### Incident-response value

If a new Log4Shell-style vulnerability appears and there are two thousand images in the registry, the SBOM attestation lets the team search signed SBOM data for affected components without pulling apart every image manually.
A signature alone can say that an image was signed, but it does not list the packages inside it.
For this to work during an incident, every image must already have a trustworthy SBOM attestation attached, the attestations must be searchable, and teams must trust the signing key and registry metadata.
Without that preparation, the attestation process would be too late for a fast three-in-the-morning response.
